p: The Hebrew says "we have heard"; the Greek and Jeremiah 49:14 say "I."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82), where the word is visible
readings.en: we have heard a report
readings.plain: We have heard a report

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (Ἀκοὴν ἤκουσα); the same verse in Jeremiah 49:14 (Hebrew shama'ti, "I have heard")
readings.en: I have heard a report
readings.plain: I have heard a report

why: The Hebrew text and the scroll agree on "we," and "we" is the harder reading, since Jeremiah has "I" and a copyist or translator would be likely to make the two alike. The Greek may have been brought into line with Jeremiah, or may be a translator's smoothing. The Mur 88 scroll has the word restored in brackets in the printout, so it is not cited.

a: an envoy was sent among the nations
p: The Greek has a word for siege or enclosure where the Hebrew has "envoy," and says "to Idumea."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008)
readings.en: and an envoy was sent among the nations
readings.plain: an envoy was sent among the nations

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (περιοχήν)
readings.orig: καὶ περιοχὴν εἰς τὰ ἔθνη ἐξαπέστειλεν
readings.en: and a siege/enclosure he sent out to the nations
readings.plain: a siege was sent out against the nations

why: Hebrew tsir (messenger) is the same word as in Jeremiah 49:14. The Greek translator seems to have read or guessed a word for a ring of siege, which does not suit the sentence. The Greek also writes "Idumea," the Greek name for Edom, as the translator's own usage. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: your nest is set among the stars
p: One Dead Sea scroll and the Greek read "you set your nest"; the Masoretic Text has a bare form that reads "is set."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); Mur 88 (Wadi Murabba'at Minor Prophets scroll)
readings.en: your nest is set
readings.plain: your nest is set among the stars

readings.w: 4QXIIg (4Q82), as read in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription; the Greek (θῇς) also has a verb "you set"
readings.en: you set your nest
readings.plain: you set your nest among the stars

why: The meaning is nearly the same either way. The Masoretic reading (an unusual bare verb form) is the harder, and 4Q82 and the Greek may smooth it into a regular "you set." Mur 88 agrees with the Masoretic Text. The printout shows the scroll's word without brackets, so it is a visible reading, but a single letter.

t: "How ruined" or "where would you be thrown?"
p: The Greek reads this cry as a question about where Edom would be thrown.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82) and Mur 88, which both have the same consonants
readings.en: how you have been ruined
readings.plain: how ruined you are

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (ποῦ ἂν ἀπερρίφης)
readings.en: where would you have been thrown away?
readings.plain: where would you have been thrown away

why: Both scrolls agree with the Masoretic Text, and the Hebrew makes good sense as an outcry. The Greek has a different sense, perhaps the translator's reading of the unusual verb nidmeita (from damah, to be cut off) or a freer rendering.

a: Those who eat your bread set a trap under you
t: "Your bread": in the Hebrew, missing in the Greek
p: The Greek has no word for "your bread," and takes the next word as "ambush."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); 4QXIIg (4Q82) and Mur 88, which both have the word for "your bread"
readings.en: your bread they set a trap under you
readings.plain: Those who eat your bread set a trap under you

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (ἔθηκαν ἔνεδρα ὑποκάτω σου)
readings.en: they set an ambush under you
readings.plain: They set an ambush under you

why: Two ancient Hebrew scrolls and the Masoretic Text have "your bread." The Greek may have passed over a puzzling phrase. The Plain keeps it and reads it as the men who share Edom's table.

t: Where does verse 9 end? (goes with verse 10)
p: The Hebrew puts "by slaughter" at the end of verse 9. The Greek puts it at the start of verse 10.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008) (verse division); 4Q82 and Mur 88, which have the word in the printout's verse 9, though scrolls carry no verse numbers
readings.en: cut off by slaughter
readings.plain: is cut off by slaughter

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (διὰ τὴν σφαγὴν, in verse 10)
readings.en: is cut off
readings.plain: is cut off

why: The Masoretic Text ends verse 9 with miqqatel, "by slaughter," and the Plain follows it. The Greek takes the word with the reason clause that begins verse 10 ("because of the slaughter and the wrongdoing against your brother Jacob"). The two verses go together; see the entry at verse 10. The scrolls have no verse numbers, so the printout can only follow the Masoretic division.

a: You did violence to your brother Jacob
p: The Greek begins verse 10 with "because of the slaughter and the wrongdoing."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); Mur 88 (words visible only in part); 4Q82 spells "your brother" and "cover you" with a long ending (-kah)
readings.en: from violence to your brother Jacob
readings.plain: You did violence to your brother Jacob

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (διὰ τὴν σφαγὴν καὶ τὴν ἀσέβειαν ἀδελφοῦ σου Ἰακώβ)
readings.orig: διὰ τὴν σφαγὴν καὶ τὴν ἀσέβειαν
readings.en: because of the slaughter and the wrongdoing against your brother Jacob
readings.plain: Because of the slaughter and the wrongdoing against your brother Jacob

why: The Greek moves "slaughter" over from verse 9 and renders chamas (violence) as asebeia (godlessness, wrongdoing). The Hebrew is clear and the scroll's spelling differences are only spelling. This entry goes with the one at verse 9.

p: The text is written "his gate" and read "his gates." A Dead Sea scroll has the written form.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Qere (what is read aloud); the Greek (πύλας, plural)
readings.en: his gates
readings.plain: through his gates

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Ketiv (what is written in the Leningrad Codex); Mur 88, which also has the shorter spelling
readings.en: his gate
readings.plain: through his gate

why: The Leningrad Codex writes "his gate" but marks it to be read "his gates." Mur 88 has the shorter spelling, which can also be read as a plural without a yod. The difference is slight: a conquered city's gate or gates. The Plain follows the read form and the Greek. In 4Q82 the word is restored in brackets, so the scroll is not cited.

p: The Greek turns the Hebrew "his misfortune" into "the day of strangers."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008)
readings.en: on the day of his misfortune
readings.plain: the day of his misfortune

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (ἀλλοτρίων)
readings.en: on the day of strangers
readings.plain: the day of strangers

why: Hebrew nokhro is related to the root nkr, "foreign, strange," and the Greek translator took it in that sense. This is a difference in how the word was understood, not in its consonants. The Plain follows the sense "misfortune," which fits the parallel lines.

a: Do not look with delight at their trouble
t: Gate, gathering and help in the attack
p: The Greek gives a different sense to three words in verse 13.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008)
readings.en: do not look, you too, on his calamity ... do not stretch out against his wealth
readings.plain: Do not look with delight at their trouble

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (συναγωγήν; συνεπιθῇ; δύναμιν)
readings.orig: μηδὲ ἐπίδῃς καὶ σὺ τὴν συναγωγὴν αὐτῶν ... μηδὲ συνεπιθῇ ἐπὶ τὴν δύναμιν αὐτῶν
readings.en: do not look, you too, on their gathering ... do not join in the attack on their force
readings.plain: Do not look, you too, on their gathering ... Do not join in the attack on their force

why: The Greek has "their gathering" for Hebrew ra'ato (his calamity), "do not join in the attack" for tishlachnah (stretch out), and "force" for chelo (wealth, strength; compare verse 11). The sense of the Hebrew is clear, and the Greek differences look like a translator's interpretation. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: They will drink, they will gulp it down
p: The Greek has "drink and go down" where the Hebrew has a rare verb.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); Mur 88, which has the verse in part
readings.en: and they will drink and gulp
readings.plain: They will drink, they will gulp it down

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (πίονται καὶ καταβήσονται)
readings.en: they will drink and come down
readings.plain: They will drink and go down

why: The Hebrew la'u is rare and the Greek translator seems to have read or guessed a different verb. "Gulp" fits a drinking scene, and the Masoretic Text is the only Hebrew witness. 4Q82 does not preserve this verse.

t: "Their property" or "those who took it from them"?
p: The same consonants can be read "their possessions" or "those who dispossessed them." The Greek and a scroll point to the second.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008) (pointed morasheihem)
readings.en: their possessions
readings.plain: take over their own property

readings.w: Mur 88 (written with a yod, מורישיהם, which allows "their dispossessors"); the Greek (τοὺς κατακληρονομήσαντας αὐτούς, "those who took possession of them")
readings.en: those who dispossessed them
readings.plain: take over those who took them over

why: The Masoretic vowels give a good sense, a repeat of "take over" in the same line. But the Greek understood the word as a person who takes possession, and Mur 88 spells it with a yod, which fits that reading and was ambiguous before vowel marks existed. The question cannot be settled from the consonants. The Plain keeps the Masoretic reading, and the other is a real possibility.

a: No one will be left of the house of Esau
p: The Greek has a word meaning "bearing fire" or "bearing grain" where the Hebrew has "survivor."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008)
readings.en: and there will be no survivor to the house of Esau
readings.plain: No one will be left of the house of Esau

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (πυροφόρος)
readings.orig: καὶ οὐκ ἔσται πυροφόρος τῷ οἴκῳ Ἠσαύ
readings.en: and there will be no fire-bearer (or grain-bearer) to the house of Esau
readings.plain: and there will be no one bearing fire to the house of Esau

why: Hebrew sarid (survivor, one left) appears in the Greek as pyrophoros, which is probably a loose rendering or a guess at the word. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the fire-word may have been prompted by the verb "will be burned" in the same verse.

t: "The field of Ephraim" and the Shephelah
p: The Greek reads "the mountain of Ephraim" and leaves the Shephelah as a name.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008)
readings.en: the field of Ephraim ... and the Shephelah
readings.plain: the people of the Shephelah

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (ὄρος Ἐφράιμ; Σεφηλά)
readings.orig: τὸ ὄρος Ἐφράιμ ... οἱ ἐν τῇ Σεφηλά
readings.en: the mountain of Ephraim ... those in the Shephelah (a name)
readings.plain: the mountain of Ephraim ... those in the Shephelah

why: The Greek reads Hebrew sedeh ("field, region") as "mountain" and writes the Hebrew shefelah as a name (Sephela) instead of translating it. The differences do not change the map. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

p: The Greek reads "the beginning" where the Hebrew has an unclear word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); Mur 88, which has the words visible with the same consonants
readings.en: this host (or rampart)
readings.plain: this army of Israelites

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (τῆς μετοικεσίας ἡ ἀρχὴ αὕτη)
readings.en: this beginning
readings.plain: this first part of the Israelites

why: The Hebrew hachel is itself unclear, but the Masoretic Text and Mur 88 agree on the consonants. The Greek seems to have understood a different word, "beginning." The Plain follows the Hebrew and treats the verse as one of the book's hardest.

p: The Greek reads "as far as Ephrathah." The Hebrew has the place name Sepharad.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008); Mur 88, where the word is visible with the same consonants
readings.en: in Sepharad
readings.plain: Sepharad

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (ἕως Ἐφράθα)
readings.en: as far as Ephrathah
readings.plain: Ephrathah

why: Sepharad is a rare, unfamiliar name, and the Greek translator seems to have replaced it with Ephrathah, a name from the Bethlehem area. Mur 88 shows the Hebrew name.

p: The Greek reads "those who are saved"; the Hebrew has a word for "rescuers."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008) (moshi'im)
readings.en: rescuers
readings.plain: Rescuers

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (ἀνασωζόμενοι); Mur 88 has a shorter spelling that could be read either way
readings.en: those who are saved, survivors
readings.plain: Survivors

why: The Hebrew moshi'im is the word for the judges who saved Israel. The Greek understood a passive form, "those who have been saved." Mur 88 writes the word without a vav (mshy'ym), which does not decide between the readings. The Plain follows the Hebrew, as the active sense suits "to judge Mount Esau."

p: The Greek has "from Mount Zion, to take vengeance on Mount Esau," where the Hebrew has "on Mount Zion, to judge."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, about AD 1008)
readings.orig: וְעָלוּ מוֹשִׁעִים בְּהַר צִיּוֹן לִשְׁפֹּט אֶת־הַר עֵשָׂו
readings.en: and deliverers will go up on Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau
readings.plain: to judge Mount Esau

readings.w: Greek (as printed by Swete) (ἐξ ὄρους Σειών; ἐκδικῆσαι)
readings.orig: ἀναβήσονται ἀνασωζόμενοι ἐξ ὄρους Σειὼν τοῦ ἐκδικῆσαι τὸ ὄρος Ἠσαύ
readings.en: survivors will go up from Mount Zion to avenge Mount Esau
readings.plain: Survivors will go up from Mount Zion to take vengeance on Mount Esau

why: Two differences. The Greek has "from" for Hebrew be- ("on"), and ekdikesai ("to avenge, to execute justice on") for lishpot ("to judge, rule"). The Greek verb narrows the Hebrew to vengeance and, with "survivors" for "rescuers" (see the entry at "Rescuers"), points to the saved themselves and not to leaders who act for them. The Hebrew shaphat can mean rule as well as judge, and the Plain follows it. How a reader takes this verse (leaders, a Messiah, or the saved) is affected by the choice.
